title: Feature Engineering
blurb: Tests scaling, skew transforms, polynomial and binned features, categorical and target encoding, cyclical datetime features and keeping every fitted step leakage-safe, mostly by computing the values by hand.

ideas.title: Log and power transforms for skewed data
One-hot, ordinal, label and frequency encoding

questions.prompt: A customer's features include income (tens of thousands) and age (tens). For which model can you skip feature scaling?
options: An SVM with an RBF kernel
A Random Forest
Logistic regression with an L2 penalty
k-nearest neighbours
questions.explanation: Trees split on thresholds such as "income > 52,000". Rescaling a feature moves the threshold but sends the same rows to each side, so the tree is unchanged. KNN and the RBF SVM use distances, which income would dominate. The L2 penalty on logistic regression punishes coefficients by size, so it is also scale-sensitive.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter reach for `np.log1p` rather than `np.log` on right-skewed features such as income or price?
options: `log1p` output is unit-free, so no later scaling is ever needed
`log1p` stretches the right tail so the outliers stand out more clearly
`log1p` turns any skewed distribution into an exact normal distribution
$\log(1+x)$ is 0 at $x=0$, so zero values do not become minus infinity
questions.explanation: `np.log(0)` is $-\infty$, which breaks most models. `np.log1p(0) = 0`. Both transforms compress the right tail rather than stretch it. The log of lognormal data, as in Listing 14.1, is normal. Other skewed shapes stay non-normal after the log.

questions.prompt: A target peaks when $X$ is near 1 and falls away on both sides. A linear regression given only $X$ fits poorly. What does the chapter do to fix this without changing the model?
options: Add a squared term, such as $(X-1)^2$, as a new feature
Apply `np.log1p` to $X$ to compress its long right tail
Label-encode $X$ into integer bins before fitting the line
Standardise $X$ so the model sees every value on a unit scale
questions.explanation: A linear model draws a straight line in whatever features it is given. With $(X-1)^2$ as a feature, the relationship becomes linear (the chapter's correlation goes from 0.62 to $-0.99$). Standardising is a linear rescale, so it cannot bend the line. A log is monotonic, so it cannot create a peak either.

questions.prompt: Why is integer label encoding of a nominal column (say `city` with codes 0, 1, 2) risky when the model is linear?
options: It copies the target into the feature, so the scores become optimistic
The model reads codes as amounts, so city 2 counts as twice city 1
It creates one column per city, so the feature matrix grows too wide
Linear models cannot accept integer columns and raise an error
questions.explanation: A linear model multiplies the code by one coefficient, which forces an order and equal spacing that do not exist. Trees can cope because they split the codes into groups. One column per city is one-hot encoding, not label encoding. Label encoding does not use the target, so it does not leak.

questions.prompt: What does target encoding put in place of each category, and why does the chapter insist on fold-holdout?
options: A random integer per category, redrawn in each fold, so no false order is implied between categories
The category's mean target computed on the other folds, so no row sees its own label
The number of rows in that category, computed on the test set, so rare categories are flagged before training
The mean target for that category over the whole dataset, so each estimate uses as much data as possible
questions.explanation: Target encoding uses the label, so a naive global mean lets each training row see its own answer, and the test rows' answers too. Fold-holdout encoding (Listing 14.5) computes each row's value from the other folds. A count is frequency encoding, which has no leakage risk.

questions.prompt: Why does Listing 14.6 add `hour_sin` and `hour_cos` rather than relying on the raw hour integer?
options: Raw integers put 23:00 and 00:00 23 units apart, but on the circle they are neighbours
sin and cos turn the hour into a categorical feature that a tree can split on
sin and cos rescale the hour into $[0, 1]$, which is what bounded-input models need
One of sin or cos carries all the information, and the other is a spare copy for checking
questions.explanation: Hour is cyclical. Mapping $\theta = 2\pi h/24$ onto $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ keeps neighbouring hours close, including across midnight. The values lie in $[-1, 1]$, not $[0, 1]$. Both are needed, because sin alone gives the same value to two different hours.

questions.prompt: Which order of steps scales features without leaking test information?
options: Split, then call `fit_transform` on the training rows and `fit_transform` again on the test rows
Split, fit the scaler on training rows, then transform train and test with it
Fit the scaler on all rows, transform them, then split into train and test
Split, fit the scaler on the test rows, then transform the training rows with it
questions.explanation: Scaling is part of the model. Its statistics must come from training data only and then be applied, never refitted, to test data. Fitting before the split leaks test statistics. Refitting on test gives test rows a different scale from the one the model learned on.

questions.prompt: A training column holds $[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]$. `StandardScaler` uses the mean and the population std ($\div n$). What is the scaled value of 50? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation:
Mean $= 30$. Squared deviations are $400, 100, 0, 100, 400$, sum 1000. Variance $= 1000/5 = 200$, so $\sigma = \sqrt{200} \approx 14.142$.
$$z = (50 - 30)/14.142 \approx 1.414$$
Using the sample std ($\div 4$, $\sigma \approx 15.81$) gives 1.265, which is not what `StandardScaler` does.

questions.prompt: The Box-Cox transform, a generalisation of the log, is $x^{(\lambda)} = (x^{\lambda} - 1)/\lambda$ for $\lambda \ne 0$ and $\ln x$ for $\lambda = 0$ (defined for $x > 0$). With $\lambda = 0.5$, what does $x = 100$ become? Give a decimal to 1 d.p.
questions.explanation:
$$\frac{100^{0.5} - 1}{0.5} = \frac{10 - 1}{0.5} = 18.0$$
For comparison, $x = 16$ becomes $(4-1)/0.5 = 6.0$. The raw gap of 84 shrinks to 12. With $\lambda = 0$ (the log) the two values become 2.77 and 4.61, a gap of 1.83. Smaller $\lambda$ compresses the right tail harder, and `PowerTransformer` picks $\lambda$ from the data.

questions.prompt: A linear model has 4 numeric features. You add `PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)`. How many columns come out? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: Output = 4 original features + 4 squares + $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ pairwise interactions $= 14$. With `interaction_only=True` the squares are dropped, leaving $4 + 6 = 10$. Column counts grow fast with degree and feature count, which is the overfitting risk in §14.3.

questions.prompt: A `ColumnTransformer` one-hot encodes `region` (5 values) and `payment_method` (4 values) with `OneHotEncoder(drop='first')`, ordinal-encodes `size` (small/medium/large) into one column, and scales `age` and `items_in_cart`. How many columns does it output? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: With `drop='first'`, a column with $c$ values gives $c-1$ dummies: $4 + 3 = 7$. Ordinal encoding gives 1 column. The two numeric columns stay 2. Total $7 + 1 + 2 = 10$. Without `drop='first'` it would be 12. Note that `size` is ordered, so one ordinal column is the right encoding for it.

questions.prompt: Using Listing 14.5's smoothing formula with `smoothing=10`, a category appears 4 times in the other folds with mean target 0.75. The global mean is 0.20. What is the smoothed encoding? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation:
$$\frac{\text{mean} \times \text{count} + \text{global} \times m}{\text{count} + m} = \frac{0.75 \times 4 + 0.20 \times 10}{4 + 10} = \frac{3 + 2}{14} \approx 0.357$$
With only 4 rows, the estimate is pulled most of the way back towards the global mean. A category with 400 rows would stay close to its own mean.

questions.prompt: Using Listing 14.6, what is `hour_sin` for an order placed at 20:00? Give a decimal to 3 d.p.
questions.explanation:
$\theta = 2\pi \times 20/24 = 5\pi/3$ (300°).
$$\sin(5\pi/3) = -\sqrt{3}/2 \approx -0.866$$
And `hour_cos` $= \cos(5\pi/3) = 0.5$. A common slip is to use degrees in `np.sin`, which expects radians.

questions.prompt:
What is wrong with this code?
```python
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_s = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_s = scaler.fit_transform(X_test)
model.fit(X_train_s, y_train)
print(model.score(X_test_s, y_test))
```
options: `scaler.fit_transform(X_train)` should be `scaler.transform(X_train)`, because the scaler is not yet fitted
`model.fit` should receive the unscaled `X_train`, and only the test rows should be scaled
The split must come after scaling, so that train and test share one scale
`scaler.fit_transform(X_test)` refits the scaler on test data. It should be `scaler.transform(X_test)`
questions.explanation: The second `fit_transform` learns a new mean and std from the test rows, so test data is scaled differently from the data the model learned on, and test statistics enter the evaluation. The chapter's rule is split first, `.fit()` on train only, `.transform()` on test. Fitting on the training rows is correct. Scaling before the split is the leak the chapter warns against.

questions.prompt: A training column holds $[3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 100]$. `RobustScaler` subtracts the median and divides by the IQR. With NumPy's default (linear) percentiles, $Q_1 = 5.25$ and $Q_3 = 8.5$. What does the value 9 become? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation:
Median $= (6+7)/2 = 6.5$. IQR $= 8.5 - 5.25 = 3.25$.
$$(9 - 6.5)/3.25 \approx 0.77$$
Compare `MinMaxScaler`: $(9-3)/(100-3) \approx 0.062$. The single outlier squashes the five normal values into $[0, 0.062]$. `RobustScaler` keeps them spread out, and the outlier becomes $(100-6.5)/3.25 \approx 28.8$. That is why the Quick Reference marks MinMax as "very" sensitive to outliers.

questions.prompt: Prices are $[0, 9, 99, 999]$. You take `np.log1p`, average the four logged values, then map back with `np.expm1`. What value do you get? Give a decimal to 1 d.p.
questions.explanation:
The logs are $\ln 1, \ln 10, \ln 100, \ln 1000 = 0, 2.303, 4.605, 6.908$. Their mean is 3.454.
$$e^{3.454} - 1 \approx 31.62 - 1 = 30.6$$
The raw mean is 276.75, pulled up by 999. The mean on the log scale maps back to a geometric-style centre, close to the typical value. This is why the chapter's logged income has mean and median nearly equal. It also warns that a model trained on log targets predicts this kind of centre, not the raw mean.

questions.prompt:
What does the last line print?
```python
ages = pd.Series([12, 18, 19, 35, 36, 60, 61, 17, 35, 50])
bands = pd.cut(ages, bins=[0, 18, 35, 60, 120])
print((bands == pd.Interval(18, 35)).sum())
```
Give an integer.
questions.explanation: `pd.cut` intervals are closed on the right by default, so the bands are $(0,18], (18,35], (35,60], (60,120]$. The band $(18, 35]$ holds 19, 35 and 35, so the count is 3. Age 18 falls in $(0, 18]$ and 36 falls in $(35, 60]$. Assuming left-closed bins gives 2 (18 and 19) and is the usual slip.

questions.prompt:
What does this print?
```python
enc = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore', sparse_output=False)
enc.fit(pd.DataFrame({'region': ['north', 'south', 'east']}))
print(enc.transform(pd.DataFrame({'region': ['west']})))
```
options: `[[nan nan nan]]`
A `ValueError` about the unknown category `west`
questions.explanation: The encoder learned three categories. With `handle_unknown='ignore'`, an unseen value gets all zeros in that block, so production data with a new region does not crash the pipeline. No new column is added at transform time. Without `handle_unknown='ignore'`, the default raises a `ValueError`.

questions.prompt: Listing 14.5 runs with `smoothing=2`. The global mean of `y_train` is 0.40. Row $r$ has `city = 'A'` and label 1, and sits in the current validation fold. In the *other* folds, city A appears 3 times with labels 1, 0, 0. What encoding does row $r$ receive? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation:
Out-of-fold stats for A: mean $= 1/3$, count 3.
$$\frac{(1/3)(3) + 0.40 \times 2}{3 + 2} = \frac{1 + 0.8}{5} = 0.36$$
A naive encoding that includes row $r$ sees 4 rows with labels 1, 1, 0, 0: $(2 + 0.8)/6 \approx 0.47$. The row's own positive label raised its own feature, which is exactly the leak fold-holdout removes.

questions.prompt: Using the sin/cos encoding of hour from Listing 14.6, what is the Euclidean distance between 22:00 and 02:00? (The raw hour values differ by 20.) Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation:
The hours are 4 apart around the clock, so the angle between them is $2\pi \times 4/24 = \pi/3$. Two points on a unit circle separated by angle $\Delta$ are $2\sin(\Delta/2)$ apart.
$$2\sin(\pi/6) = 2 \times 0.5 = 1.00$$
Directly: 22:00 is $(\cos, \sin) = (0.866, -0.5)$ and 02:00 is $(0.866, 0.5)$, so the distance is $1.0$. The raw integers say 20 hours apart, the circle correctly says 4.

questions.prompt: A churn model predicts on 1 March whether each customer leaves in March. The team builds RFM-style features. Select ALL features that leak.
options: Number of support tickets the customer filed during March
Product category, frequency-encoded using counts from the training rows
Region, target-encoded with churn rates computed on the full dataset, test rows included
Recency: days from the customer's last purchase before 1 March to 1 March
Order value, scaled by a `StandardScaler` fitted on train and test combined
questions.explanation: March tickets are future information at prediction time, and often a symptom of the churn itself. A global target encoding bakes test labels into training rows. A scaler fitted on combined data leaks test statistics. Recency computed up to the prediction date is the classic safe domain feature from §14.2.5. Frequency encoding uses no labels, and here it uses only training counts, so it carries no leakage risk.

questions.prompt: `MinMaxScaler` (default settings) is fitted on training ages with minimum 20 and maximum 80. A test customer is 95. What value does `transform` give? Give a decimal to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation:
$$(95 - 20)/(80 - 20) = 75/60 = 1.25$$
The default `clip=False` does not force the result into $[0, 1]$. Anything outside the training range lands outside $[0, 1]$, which breaks the "bounded input" reason for choosing MinMax. The fix is not to refit the scaler on test data. Either accept values above 1, set `clip=True`, or use a scaler that does not promise bounds.

questions.prompt: Column `colour` has 3 values and is one-hot encoded with `drop='first'`, giving dummies $d_1, d_2$. Two continuous features $x_1, x_2$ join them, and all 4 columns go through `PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)`, which outputs 14 columns. How many of those 14 columns are *useful*, meaning neither identically zero nor an exact copy of another column? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: A 0/1 dummy squared is itself: $d_1^2 = d_1$ and $d_2^2 = d_2$, two copies. The dummies are mutually exclusive, so $d_1 d_2 = 0$ for every row, one zero column. $14 - 3 = 11$. The useful interactions are the ones the chapter praises, such as $d_1 x_1$, which let the slope of $x_1$ differ by colour. Blind polynomial expansion of one-hot columns adds dead and duplicate features.

questions.prompt: Every `customer_id` in a dataset appears exactly once. A teammate target-encodes it naively on the full data, with Listing 14.5's smoothing formula and `smoothing=10`. What is the correlation between the encoded column and the target on the training rows?
options: Undefined, because single-row categories are always mapped to the global mean
Close to 0, because smoothing pulls every single-row category almost all the way to the global mean
Exactly 1, because $(y_i + 10\bar y)/11$ is a linear function of the row's own label
About 0.5, because with 10 pseudo-rows smoothing removes roughly half of the leak
questions.explanation: With count 1, the naive smoothed value is $(y_i \cdot 1 + 10\bar y)/11$. The values sit close to $\bar y$, but they are an increasing linear function of $y_i$, so the correlation is exactly 1. Smoothing shrinks the scale, not the leak, and a linear model rescales it back. Listing 14.5's fold-holdout version never sees the row's own label, so each unique ID falls back to the global mean (via `fillna`), and the column carries no signal.

questions.prompt: To save a column, a teammate keeps `hour_sin` and drops `hour_cos`. Which other hour of the day (0 to 23) gets exactly the same `hour_sin` value as 04:00? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: $\sin\theta = \sin(\pi - \theta)$. For hour $h$, $\pi - 2\pi h/24 = 2\pi(12-h)/24$, so hour $12 - h$ matches: $12 - 4 = 8$. Both give $\sin = 0.866$. Only `hour_cos` tells them apart ($+0.5$ at 04:00, $-0.5$ at 08:00). An early-morning and a mid-morning order would look identical, which is why the chapter keeps both columns.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain why tree-based models don't need feature scaling while linear and distance-based models do, using the "splits on thresholds, not magnitudes" framing from this chapter.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Tree-based models make decisions by splitting on a threshold ("is age > 35?"), and the split location adapts to whatever scale the data is already in. Multiplying a feature by 1000 just shifts where the threshold lands, without changing which points fall on which side. Linear and distance-based models combine features directly (weighted sums, Euclidean distances), so a feature on a much larger scale mechanically dominates the combination or distance calculation regardless of its actual predictive value, unless scaled to a comparable range first.

bookExercises.prompt: For each, name the correct encoding from this chapter: (a) a `size` column with values small/medium/large; (b) a `product_sku` column with 50,000 unique values feeding a linear model; (c) a `country` column with 15 unique values, no natural order.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (a) Ordinal encoding: small/medium/large has a genuine order. (b) Target or frequency encoding (CV-safe): 50,000 unique values feeding a linear model rules out one-hot (too many columns) and label encoding (implies a false order the linear model would misread). (c) One-hot encoding: 15 unique values, no natural order, is squarely in one-hot's low-cardinality nominal range.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 14.6, compute `hour_sin`/`hour_cos` for hour 23 and hour 0 by hand, and show numerically that their Euclidean distance is small, in contrast to the raw hour values, which differ by 23.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: $\text{hour\_sin}(23) = \sin(2\pi \cdot 23/24) \approx -0.259$, $\text{hour\_cos}(23) = \cos(2\pi \cdot 23/24) \approx 0.966$. $\text{hour\_sin}(0) = 0$, $\text{hour\_cos}(0) = 1$. Euclidean distance $\approx \sqrt{(-0.259 - 0)^2 + (0.966 - 1)^2} \approx \sqrt{0.067 + 0.001} \approx 0.26$, small, correctly reflecting that hour 23 and hour 0 are only one hour apart, versus the raw integer difference of 23.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 14.8's pattern, explain what result you would expect if `customer_id` were replaced with a column that directly encoded a noisy version of the label (e.g. `last_order_value_rounded`): would the leaky-vs-safe CV $R^2$ gap this chapter measured (0.872 vs. 0.870) likely grow, shrink, or stay about the same?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Replacing `customer_id` with a column that directly (if noisily) encodes the label would very likely make the leaky-vs-safe gap grow substantially larger than 0.872 vs. 0.870. Per the Worked Example's explanation, leakage's damage scales with how strongly the leaking column correlates with the target once leaked. A column that's essentially a disguised version of the label is about as strongly correlated as a feature can be, so naive (leaky) encoding would likely produce a dramatically inflated CV score that collapses on the true held-out test set, unlike the mild, honest gap measured for the genuinely weakly-predictive `customer_id`.

bookExercises.prompt: A teammate wants to one-hot encode a `product_id` column with 8,000 unique values "to keep things simple." Using this chapter's cardinality guidance, write the two or three sentences you'd say instead.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "8,000 one-hot columns will blow up training time and memory for very little benefit. Most product IDs will appear too rarely for the model to learn anything reliable about that specific dummy column, and you'll be feeding the model 8,000 mostly-empty columns instead of a compact signal. Frequency encoding or CV-safe target encoding captures the useful signal in one column instead."

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter's measured leaky-vs-safe gap was small (0.872 vs. 0.870). Using the Worked Example's explanation for why, describe a realistic feature (not `customer_id`) in the same order dataset that would very likely produce a much larger leakage gap if encoded naively.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A column like `last_order_value_rounded` (or any feature that's derived from, or closely tracks, the order value itself after the fact) would be a strong candidate. If such a column existed and were naively target-encoded (or even just included as a raw feature) without checking whether it's actually available before the order value is known, it would very likely produce a large, disqualifying leaky-vs-safe gap, since it's effectively leaking the label back into the features.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the scikit-learn `TargetEncoder` documentation (or `category_encoders.TargetEncoder`). Identify one detail of its built-in cross-fitting behaviour that differs from Procedure 14.2's hand-written version, and explain what problem that difference solves.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. sklearn's built-in `TargetEncoder` (added in recent sklearn versions) performs its cross-fitting internally and automatically during `.fit_transform()`, choosing fold splits and smoothing parameters without the user hand-writing the loop. This removes the risk of a manual implementation bug (e.g. an off-by-one in fold indexing, or accidentally using `.fit_transform()` instead of separate `.fit()`/`.transform()` calls) that could silently reintroduce leakage in a hand-rolled version like Procedure 14.2's.
